hints: Picture heating magnesium strongly in pure oxygen, think about how vigorous and exothermic this combustion is and what kind of light and solid residue such a reaction would leave.
walkthrough:
Visualise burning magnesium**
You have seen magnesium ribbon burn in air, and in pure oxygen it is even more vigorous. This is a very exothermic combustion, so think light energy given out and a new solid forming. You need to state what you would actually see, not the names of chemicals.

Pick out the two key observations**
First, the flame is dazzling bright white, so bright you should not look directly at it. Second, the shiny metal disappears and is replaced by a crumbly white or light grey solid, which is magnesium oxide ash or powder, sometimes seen as white smoke.
Final answer: Burns with a bright white light / flame to form a white / grey solid / ash / powder.

hints: Remember that magnesium oxide is a basic oxide, so with hydrochloric acid it will form a magnesium salt plus water, think about which salt and how many moles of acid are needed.
walkthrough:
Identify the acid base partners**
Excess $\text{HCl}$ in the stomach is the acid. $\text{MgO}$ is a metal oxide, so it acts as a base. A base plus an acid gives a salt plus water. Here the salt must contain magnesium and chloride, so it is $\text{MgCl}_{2}$.

Balance the equation**
Write $\text{MgO} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ first, then check atoms. You need two chlorides on the right in $\text{MgCl}_{2}$, so you need $2\text{HCl}$ on the left. That also gives $2\text{H}$ and $1\text{O}$ on each side to make $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. The balanced equation is $\text{MgO} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Think of the general name given when an acid reacts with a base, alkali, metal oxide or carbonate to form a salt and water and the acid is cancelled out.
walkthrough:
Link acid plus base to its name**
In (b)(i) an acid, $\text{HCl}$, is removed by a base, $\text{MgO}$, to make a neutral salt solution of $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ and water. Whenever an acid reacts with a base to form a salt plus water, we call this neutralisation.

hints: Recall the structure of solid magnesium oxide, think about how $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$ ions are arranged and whether it is simple molecular or giant.
Consider what has to be broken for the solid to melt and how the charge and strength of the ionic bonds affect the energy needed.
walkthrough:
State the structure clearly**
Solid $\text{MgO}$ is not made of separate $\text{MgO}$ molecules. It is a giant ionic lattice with $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$ ions packed in a regular repeating 3D arrangement, each ion surrounded by oppositely charged ions.

Explain why melting needs high temperature**
To melt, you must break apart that lattice enough for ions to move. That means overcoming many strong electrostatic attractions between $2+$ and $2-$ ions in all directions. These are very strong bonds because of the high charges, so a very large amount of thermal energy is needed, giving a very high melting point.

Final answer: Magnesium oxide has a giant ionic lattice / structure.
Strong ionic bonds / strong electrostatic attractions need a large amount of energy to break on melting.

hints: Think about what happens when a Group 2 carbonate is heated alone, one solid product stays behind and one gaseous product escapes, recall the products from magnesium carbonate.
walkthrough:
Work out the products and states**
Heating $\text{MgCO}_{3}$ splits it into two parts. The metal stays with oxygen as solid $\text{MgO(s)}$, and carbon dioxide is released as $\text{CO}_{2}\text{(g)}$. The starting carbonate is a solid, $\text{MgCO}_{3}\text{(s)}$.

Write the balanced equation**
One formula unit gives one of each product, so it is already balanced: $\text{MgCO}_{3}\text{(s)} \rightarrow \text{MgO(s)} + \text{CO}_{2}\text{(g)}$. Always include the state symbols as requested.

hints: Recall the name used when a single compound is broken down into simpler substances by heating alone, as with carbonates and hydroxides.
walkthrough:
Recognise breakdown by heat**
Here one compound, $\text{MgCO}_{3}$, is split into two simpler substances, $\text{MgO}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}$, using heat only. Breaking down a compound by heating is called thermal decomposition. The word thermal simply emphasises that heat causes it.
